In [[vector calculus]], '''Chandrasekhar–Wentzel lemma''' was derived by [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] and [[Gregor Wentzel]] in 1965, while studying the stability of rotating liquid drop.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Chandrasekhar |first=S. |year=1965 |title=The Stability of a Rotating Liquid Drop |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |volume=286 |issue=1404 |pages=1–26 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1965.0127 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Chandrasekhar |first=S. |last2=Wali |first2=K. C. |year=2001 |title=A Quest for Perspectives: Selected Works of S. Chandrasekhar: With Commentary |publisher=World Scientific }}</ref> The lemma states that ''if <math>\mathbf S</math> is a surface bounded by a simple closed contour <math>C</math>, then''

:<math>\mathbf L = \oint_C \mathbf x\times(d\mathbf x\times\mathbf n) = -\int_{\mathbf S}(\mathbf x\times\mathbf n)\nabla\cdot\mathbf n\ dS.</math>

Here <math>\mathbf x</math> is the position vector and <math>\mathbf n</math> is the unit normal on the surface. An immediate consequence is that if <math>\mathbf S</math> is a closed surface, then the [[line integral]] tends to zero, leading to the result,

:<math> \int_{\mathbf S}(\mathbf x\times\mathbf n)\nabla\cdot\mathbf n\ dS =0,
</math>

or, in index notation, we have

:<math>\int_{\mathbf S}x_j\nabla\cdot\mathbf n\ dS_k = \int_{\mathbf S} x_k \nabla \cdot \mathbf n\ dS_j.</math>

That is to say the tensor

:<math>T_{ij} = \int_{\mathbf S}x_j\nabla\cdot\mathbf n\ dS_i</math>

defined on a closed surface is always symmetric, i.e., <math>T_{ij}=T_{ji}</math>.

==Proof==

Let us write the vector in index notation, but [[Einstein notation|summation convention]] will be avoided throughout the proof. Then the left hand side can be written as

:<math>L_i = \oint_C [dx_i(n_jx_j+n_kx_k) + dx_j(-n_ix_j)+dx_k(-n_ix_k)]. </math>

Converting the line integral to [[surface integral]] using [[Stokes's theorem]], we get

:<math>L_i = \int_{\mathbf S} \left\{n_i\left[\frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}(-n_ix_k) - \frac{\partial }{\partial x_k}(-n_ix_j)\right] + n_j \left[\frac{\partial }{\partial x_k}(n_jx_j+n_kx_k) - \frac{\partial }{\partial x_i}(-n_ix_k)\right] + n_k\left[\frac{\partial }{\partial x_i}(-n_ix_j) - \frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}(n_jx_j+n_kx_k)\right]\right\}\ dS.</math>

Carrying out the requisite differentiation and after some rearrangement, we get

:<math>L_i = \int_{\mathbf S} \left[-\frac{1}{2}x_k\frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}(n_i^2+n_k^2) + \frac{1}{2} x_j\frac{\partial }{\partial x_k}(n_i^2+n_j^2)+n_jx_k\left(\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial x_i} + \frac{\partial n_k}{\partial x_k}\right) - n_kx_j \left(\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial x_i} + \frac{\partial n_j}{\partial x_j}\right)\right]\ dS,</math>

or, in other words,

:<math>L_i = \int_{\mathbf S} \left[\frac{1}{2} \left(x_j\frac{\partial }{\partial x_k}-x_k\frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}\right) |\mathbf n|^2 - (x_jn_k-x_kn_j)\nabla\cdot\mathbf n\right]\ dS.</math>

And since <math>|\mathbf n|^2=1</math>, we have

:<math>L_i = - \int_{\mathbf S}(x_jn_k-x_kn_j)\nabla\cdot\mathbf n\ dS,</math>

thus proving the lemma.
